newsitem.title: USA: Stratcor invests in South Africa and US vanadium.
newsitem.headline: Stratcor invests in South Africa and US vanadium.

text.p: Strategic Metals Corp, the Western world's second largest vanadium producer, said it will raise output in Hot Springs, Ark, and hike processing capacity at its Vametco operation in Brits, South Africa.
"Our objective is not to produce the greatest number of pounds, but we think we are the most profitable," Stratcor's president, William Beattie told reporters.
In South Africa Stratcor will spend $1 million to hike Brits' ability to convert pentoxide into Nitrovan, a vanadium product used in making high strength, low alloy (HSLA) steels.
A further, unspecified sum spent on environmental improvements at Vametco were also a significant cost addition, but Nitrovan would still be competitive, Beattie said.
The 25 percent process expansion at Brits will be completed by year end.
Steelmakers save 20-40 percent on vanadium bills by using Nitrovan instead of conventional ferro-vanadium, Beattie claimed.
The global vanadium market is 130 million pounds of which 100 million is consumed by steelmakers, Stratcor said.
The investment will enable all of Brits 10 million pounds of vanadium pentoxide output to be converted into higher value Nitrovan if required.

In the U.S. Stratcor will spend up to $2 million on its Hot Springs plant on equipment to extract two million pounds a year of vanadium pentoxide from Orimulsion ash, for conversion in ferro-vanadium.
Capacity at Hot Springs is 12 million pounds with production in 1997 rising to 11 million as the new processing facility comes on stream mid-year, with the aim of reaching 12 million pounds in 1998.
Stratcor is currently producing vanadium pentoxide at the annual rate of 20 million pounds, but this will rise to 30 million pounds within five years as more ash is processed.
Ash is a residue from burning Orimulsion, the bitumen-water mix fuel for power stations sold by Petroleos de Venezuela through its Bitor-Europe subsidiary.
Stratcor and Bitor-Europe, have a 50/50 share in Orbit Metallurgical. The initial source of ash will be from the Asnes power plant in Denmark.

The ash contains 19 percent vanadium, 13 percent magnesium, and 2.3 percent nickel. It has not been decided if the magnesium and nickel will be recovered at Hot Springs or at an outside conversion plant in Europe.
No vanadium has been extracted from ash on a commercial basis yet, Beattie said.
Orbit plans to build a major new facility in Europe that can recover 6 million pounds of vanadium pentoxide a year, operational by 1999.
"Bitor forecasts that up to 20 million tons of Orimulsion fuel will be burned per year worldwide by 2005, yielding 20 million pounds of vanadium pentoxide per year," Beattie said.
Plans to convert coal powered stations to Orimulsion have proved controversial among environmentalists in the U.K., but Beattie said the opposition was not based on technology, but on politics.

Orbit originally planned to open a commercial plant this year in Hennstedt, Germany to recover vanadium and other metals from ash, but this has been put on hold due to the lack of adequate ash supplies, Beattie said.
